controls.label: Elevation

Native spacing is about 463 m; the publisher interpolated gaps. The areoid is a gravity-based reference surface, not a fixed-radius sphere.
controls.notes: Mars has no global ocean. Its reference level, called the areoid, follows gravity and plays a role similar to sea level on Earth. Meters above the GMM-2B areoid. The source spacing is about 463 m, and the publisher filled gaps by interpolation. This globe shows a coarser sample of that grid. Gray grid marks missing source data.

controls.label: Albedo
controls.qualification: MGS TES bolometric Lambert albedo · 8 pixels per degree · Christensen et al. (2001)
controls.notes: How much sunlight the ground reflects, from 0 (none) to 1 (all), measured by the TES visible and near-infrared bolometer (0.3–2.9 µm) on Mars Global Surveyor. Dark regions such as Syrtis Major are dust-poor; bright regions such as Tharsis and Arabia are dust-covered. The source grid is 8 pixels per degree, about 7.4 km. TES did not observe poleward of about 87°; the publisher filled those cells with a constant 0.06, shown here as missing data.

facts.label: What it shows
facts.value: The fraction of sunlight the ground reflects across visible and near-infrared light. Dust makes Mars bright; sand and rock make it dark.

facts.label: Reading the scale
facts.value: Lambert albedo from 0.06 to 0.32, the range of the source grid. Purple is darker ground; yellow is brighter ground.

facts.label: How it was measured
facts.value: The Thermal Emission Spectrometer on Mars Global Surveyor measured reflected sunlight between 0.3 and 2.9 µm; the ASU TES team gridded the values at 8 pixels per degree.

facts.label: Limits
facts.value: Each cell is about 7.4 km across and averages many observations, so seasonal dust changes are smoothed together.

facts.label: Coverage

controls.label: Thermal inertia
controls.qualification: MGS TES nightside thermal inertia, Putzig & Mellon (2007), PDS MGS-M-TES-5-TIMAP-V1.0 product GLOBAL_TI_NIGHT_2007, 20 pixels per degree; interpolated cells withheld.
controls.notes: How slowly the ground heats by day and cools by night. Loose dust changes temperature quickly and has low thermal inertia; sand, crusted soil and rock change slowly and have high thermal inertia. Units of J m⁻² K⁻¹ s⁻½. Dusty Tharsis and Arabia sit near 10 to 50, sandy Syrtis Major near 190, Acidalia near 340. Values above 600 (0.4% of the planet) use the endpoint color. Putzig & Mellon (2007) fitted a thermal model to nightside surface temperatures measured by the Thermal Emission Spectrometer on Mars Global Surveyor, 1999–2004, and gridded the results at 20 pixels per degree (about 3 km). Each value assumes a uniform surface in the cell; layered or mixed ground gives an apparent value. Nightside coverage leaves gaps. Gray marks cells without a value and the 8.5% of the planet the producer filled by interpolation, which the product's mask flags.

controls.label: Dust cover
controls.qualification: MGS TES dust cover index, Ruff & Christensen (2002), JGR 107(E12), 5127, 16 pixels per degree; the 0.85 polar fill is withheld.
controls.notes: Where fine dust blankets the surface. A thin dust layer lowers the surface's thermal emission in one infrared band, so the index tracks dust cover rather than brightness. The authors class 0.940 or lower as dust-covered and 0.962 or higher as dust-free. Arabia reads 0.922 and Syrtis Major 0.973. Darker colors mean more dust. Ruff & Christensen (2002) averaged Thermal Emission Spectrometer emissivity between 1350 and 1400 cm⁻¹ over the mapping mission and gridded it at 16 pixels per degree. The index responds to fine particulate dust a few tens of micrometers thick; it does not measure dust depth. Gray marks the polar regions, where the published grid holds a constant fill instead of data.

controls.label: Present-day changes
controls.qualification: NASA Trek compilation of Daubar et al. (2013), Dundas et al. (2014, 2015), McEwen et al. (2014) and Ojha et al. (2014): 508 HiRISE sites.
controls.notes: Surface changes caught in repeat HiRISE images: new impact craters, craters exposing ice, gullies that changed, and recurring slope lineae (dark streaks that grow each warm season). Each coloured cell is one 5.2 km map cell holding at least one catalogued site; it is not the site's size or outline. The Trek layer combines four HiRISE catalogues; the colour follows the catalogue each site comes from. White cells hold sites from more than one. HiRISE images a small part of Mars, so unmarked ground is not proof that nothing changed. 16 of the 22 ice-exposing craters share a cell with a new-crater entry and show white. Unmarked ground is the Viking colour mosaic in grey at 35% brightness and 6 bits per channel, a presentation choice: at that level every legend colour differs by at least 15 OKLab units from 95% of the dimmed terrain. Colours come from our categorical palette, validated for all-pair separation (Trek draws every type in #d3ffbe and tells them apart by symbol shape). White, for a cell holding more than one class, is ours.

controls.notes: Deposits interpreted to contain chloride salts. Green fills the map cells whose centre lies inside a mapped deposit outline. Osterloo et al. (2010) found about 640 deposits by their distinct colour in decorrelation-stretched THEMIS infrared images and outlined each one. The salt is inferred from infrared spectra, not sampled. 347 of the 642 deposits are smaller than one 5.2 km cell and do not show; unmarked ground is not proof that no salt is there.
